claims.text: The target material is a Ta-based BCC high-entropy alloy.
The alloy is initially in a solid state.
Ab initio free-energy calculations for the target alloy are prohibitively expensive because they require thermodynamic integration over the full phase space.
The intervention uses a perturbation-based free-energy scheme with a Moment Tensor Polynomial machine-learning potential.
The MTP is trained specifically on liquid configurations at temperatures near the alloy's melting point.
The multi-component refractory liquid has a complex disordered structure.
The MTP descriptor can capture the local atomic environments of the disordered multi-component liquid without solid-state training data.
An MTP trained on representative liquid configurations approximates the liquid potential-energy surface with high fidelity.
Evaluating the MTP costs only a fraction of an ab initio energy evaluation.
Liquid-phase sampling with the MTP enables perturbative estimation of free-energy differences without a slow thermodynamic-integration path through the solid-liquid coexistence region.
Replacing full thermodynamic integration with the MTP perturbation scheme will produce more than a tenfold computational speedup.
The MTP perturbation scheme will predict free-energy differences within 5% of high-fidelity benchmarks.
The predicted accuracy and speedup depend on the liquid training set being diverse and representative.
A training set biased toward solid-like structures or low-temperature liquid states causes extrapolation errors at high temperature.
Known failure modes of TOR-TILD or related approaches in multi-component spaces cannot be established from the supplied evidence.
The accuracy of an MTP for the complex liquid structure of Ta-based high-entropy alloys remains uncertain without empirical validation.
A blind comparison at 0.9 Tm and 1.1 Tm against small-scale ab initio thermodynamic integration can test the MTP free-energy predictions.
The hypothesis is falsified if the free-energy error exceeds 10% or if the speedup is less than twofold at matched accuracy.
